author: Elijah
title: My neighbour's tree has destroyed my fence panel: Should they pay for repairs?
text:
I have a concrete panel that separates my garden and my neighbor’s garden.
However, my neighbor has a large tree that is extremely close to the fence.
The roots of the tree have deformed the post of the fence and caused a panel to fall.
Where am I standing when it comes to asking my neighbor to contribute to the repair of the fence? The fence belongs to me, according to the land registry document.
Problematic: This is the money reader is having problems with the neighbor’s tree
Jane Denton, this is money, replies: It is always a good starting point Verify the land registration documents to see where it is when it comes to ownership of the fence and limit dilemmas.
It is the duty of his neighbor to make sure that his trees do not damage his property. However, that does not mean that you can take a chainsaw and reduce your tree.
Whenever possible, try to have a face to face with your neighbor and explain the impact that your tree is having in its fence. At this point, you can also raise the problem of getting your neighbor to contribute or cover the cost of repairing your fence.
The fence fights and the relationships between the neighbors are not always simple, so it is better to know where you legally stop. I have asked three lawyers for their opinion about their problem.
Olivia Egdell-Page, partner and property director at Joseph A. Jones & Co, says: The legal position is that you have the right to cut branches or roots that cross their property from the property or public road of a neighbor, although it is better to discuss what is first proposed with its neighbor.
You can only cut the property limit. If you do more than this, your neighbor could potentially take legal actions against you for damaging your property.
If, by trimming the roots of a tree, it causes damage, although unintentionally, it will be responsible for any damage caused.
Another point to take into account if it lives in a conservation area, or if the tree in question is subject to an order of preservation of trees, is that the council may require permission to perform any tree work.
The responsibility for this crime is strict, so the person who cuts or causes damage to the tree can be processed, although the owner has a continuous responsibility to replace the protected tree.
His neighbor is responsible for maintaining his trees and hedges so that they do not damage his property, including the limits that are within his property.
Expert: Olivia Egdell-Page is a member of Joseph A. Jones & Co
If they damage his property, his neighbor would be responsible to the extent that the damage can be attributed to his actions, or not act, and so again, he would advise him to speak with his neighbor before organizing any repair work.
If they are consulted and feel included in the process, there is an argument that is more likely to cooperate with you and cover a proportion, if not all, the cost of repair or replacement.
If the initial discussions do not result in an agreement, it may consider that jointly designate an expert to analyze the problems and advise how issues can be solved or consider mediation.
If things cannot be resolved friendly, you could seek to pursue a claim against your neighbor for negligence or discomfort caused by your inability to keep the tree, or in fact you can have a claim for damage.
The law is clear in which it has the right to reduce the offensive tree, however, it must be careful before carrying out such works, particularly because it will seek a financial contribution in relation to the limit works.
Keep it friendly: Bahareh Amani says that the reader needs to talk to his neighbor before taking any measure
Are the roots of the trees invading their land? Bahareh Amani, partner of Hodge Jones and Allen, says: Your neighbor owes you to make sure your trees avoid damage to you or your property.
His neighbor would be responsible for the damage caused by his tree, or the roots of the trees, since this could be considered as a transfer of the roots in his land causing the consequent damage.
Transfer is an issue that can occur before the courts. If you decide to run for the court, you can grant a court order. They are discretionary and subject to certain rules and requirements to include whether a delay in obtaining a court order would cause more damage.
In addition, or as an alternative to a court order, the Court may grant compensation through a financial payment.
The tree and roots belong to their neighbor, however, if the roots have invaded their land, then it will have the right to eliminate the roots to prevent more damage from occurring.
However, we would advise against this, since the tree can be protected under an order of preservation of the tree or located in a conservation area. In these circumstances, it would be a crime to cut, head, LOP, uproot or damage a tree without obtaining permission from the local authority.
If it causes the tree permanently, you can be responsible before your neighbor for any damage caused to the tree. Take measures yourself and should be avoided, since an expert intervention may be required.
I suggest that you talk directly to your neighbor about the problems caused by the root damage of the tree, and ask you not only to attend to the roots of the invasted trees, but also pay to rectify the damage that has been caused to its fence.
You may not have to limit yourself to a contribution to the repair of the fence, but you can request that your neighbor pay for the total cost of repair.
Knowing: Lawyer Manjinder Kaur Atwal
Manjinder Kaur Atwal, director and lawyer at Duncan Lewis Requests, says: Since the land registration confirms that it owns the fence, its maintenance and repair generally falls.
However, that does not mean that your neighbor is out of place if your tree has caused the damage.
His neighbor has a legal duty to ensure that his tree does not cause damage to adjacent properties. If their roots have damaged their fence, they can be responsible for the cost of repairs.
However, an important decision will have to be made: can the fence be repaired without eliminating the offensive root or, in some cases, the entire tree?
If the root remains, it can cause more damage to the future, which means that any repair could be of short duration. If it is necessary to eliminate the root, this could affect the health and stability of the tree itself, which increases additional complications.
Establishing responsibility may not be direct. It is possible that you need an expert evidence of a surveyor or a arborist to confirm that the roots of the trees are responsible.
However, these reports can be expensive, so it is worth weighing if the cost of obtaining evidence exceeds the cost of simply repairing the fence.
Before considering legal actions, it is always better to raise the problem in a friendly way. Explain the situation, present any evidence and try to achieve an understanding with your neighbor.
You can ask your neighbor to contribute to repair costs or agree on preventive measures, such as the tree or install a root barrier.
However, if the root is already causing significant structural problems, elimination could be the only effective long -term solution, something that will require careful discussion and possibly an expert advice.
If your neighbor refuses to cooperate, you can explore an annoying claim, but the litigation must be a last resort.
Consider discussing long -term solutions, such as administered pruning or, if necessary, the elimination of trees. However, if the tree is protected by an order of preservation of the tree, pruning or elimination could result in a considerable fine.
In summary, while the fence is his responsibility, his neighbor can support some responsibility for the damage caused by his tree. A diplomatic approach is always better before resorting to legal actions, after all, good fences are good neighbors, but finding a fair and practical solution is better.
